group.passage: Imagine a keyboard on which every note sounds equally loud, however hard or gently you press the keys. For centuries, this was the problem facing anyone who played the harpsichord. Inside the instrument, small picks pluck the strings, so the player has almost no control over how loud each note sounds. The other keyboard of the time, the clavichord, did respond to the player’s touch, but its voice was so weak that it could hardly be heard beyond a small room. Shortly before 1700, Bartolomeo Cristofori, who looked after the musical instruments of a rich prince in Florence, set out to improve the harpsichord. His idea was to replace the plucking parts with small wooden hammers covered in leather. When a key was pressed, a hammer flew up, struck a pair of strings, and at once dropped away so that they could keep ringing. Because the hammer hit harder when the key was pressed harder, a player could now move freely between quiet and strong notes. Cristofori named his invention after this, calling it a “harpsichord with soft and loud” in Italian. In time, the name was shortened to “pianoforte” and then to “piano.” Surprisingly, the invention drew little attention at first. A journalist who saw the new instruments in Cristofori’s workshop in 1709 praised them in an article two years later, yet most composers in Italy went on writing for the harpsichord. The first printed music for the piano did not appear until 1732, more than thirty years after Cristofori had started his work. The piano’s real chance came later in the eighteenth century. Its design reached Germany and England, and music was moving out of palaces and into large public halls, where the harpsichord was of little use. Composers such as Mozart and Haydn, and later Beethoven, wanted bigger sounds and greater changes in volume, and the piano could give them both. By around 1800, it had pushed aside the two older keyboards. Today’s pianos are much larger and louder than Cristofori’s, yet his basic hammer system is still in use. Three of his pianos survive, and the oldest, made in 1720, is kept in a museum in New York.

translation_zh.text:
鋼琴的誕生

想像一架鍵盤樂器，不論你按鍵按得多用力或多輕，每個音聽起來都一樣大聲。好幾個世紀以來，這正是每個彈大鍵琴的人都會碰到的問題。在大鍵琴裡，小小的撥片撥動琴弦，所以彈奏者幾乎無法控制每個音有多大聲。當時另一種鍵盤樂器——擊弦古鋼琴——確實會隨彈奏者的觸鍵而改變，但它的聲音太微弱，出了小房間幾乎就聽不到。

1700 年前不久，替佛羅倫斯一位富有親王照管樂器的巴爾托洛梅奧‧克里斯托福里（Bartolomeo Cristofori）著手改良大鍵琴。他的構想是把撥弦的零件換成包著皮革的小木槌。按下琴鍵時，木槌會往上彈起、敲擊一對琴弦，然後立刻落下，讓琴弦能持續發聲。因為鍵按得越用力，木槌就敲得越重，彈奏者終於可以在弱音和強音之間自由變換。克里斯托福里就以這一點為他的發明命名，用義大利文稱它為「能彈弱也能彈強的大鍵琴」。後來這個名字被縮短成「pianoforte」，最後又縮成「piano」。

出人意料的是，這項發明起初很少受到注意。一位記者在 1709 年於克里斯托福里的工坊看到這些新樂器，兩年後寫文章讚揚它們，但義大利大多數的作曲家仍繼續為大鍵琴作曲。第一份印刷出版的鋼琴樂譜直到 1732 年才出現，距離克里斯托福里開始研發已經超過三十年。

鋼琴真正的機會出現在十八世紀後期。它的設計傳到了德國和英國，而音樂也正從宮廷移到大型的公共音樂廳，在那裡大鍵琴派不上什麼用場。莫札特、海頓等作曲家，以及後來的貝多芬，都想要更宏大的聲音和更鮮明的音量變化，而鋼琴兩者都能給他們。到了 1800 年前後，鋼琴已經取代了那兩種較舊的鍵盤樂器。

今天的鋼琴比克里斯托福里的大得多，也響亮得多，但他基本的擊槌系統至今仍在使用。他的鋼琴有三架留存至今，其中最古老的一架製於 1720 年，收藏在紐約的一間博物館。
